title: TypeScript SDK: Dual-consumer streaming playbook (AsyncIterator + Web Streams)
creator: Liam Chen
description:
Goal: Provide a single, formally documented pattern in the TypeScript SDK that lets application code consume streaming model outputs via either AsyncIterable<T> (for Node + modern bundlers) or Web Streams (ReadableStream) with minimal friction. Deliver a small set of ergonomic adapters, explicit retry and resume semantics for transient network errors, cancellation behavior that cleans up runtime resources (KV cache handles, in-flight batches), and example patterns for migration.

Background: We've shipped multiple streaming prototypes (AsyncIterable-first and WebStream-first) which caused user confusion. Customers writing isomorphic code need both interfaces to interop with browser Fetch-based patterns, existing async-for-of loops, and frameworks that prefer Web Streams for pipeTo/tee usage. We also must preserve our retry semantics and ensure we don't double-deliver tokens after reconnects.

Scope and non-goals:
- In scope: adapters (AsyncIterable <-> ReadableStream), core consumer contract, deterministic retry boundaries, small example app + docs, tests (unit + integration), migration guide.
- Out of scope: changing server protocol, implementing long-term persistence-based checkpointing, adding new language SDKs (Python/Go handled separately).

Design decisions and trade-offs: 
1) Adapter strategy: create a canonical internal stream source represented as an internal AsyncGenerator that owns decoding/parsing and retry checkpoints. Expose two thin surface adapters: toAsyncIterable(source) returns AsyncIterable<string | TokenChunk>, and toReadableStream(source) constructs a ReadableStream by pulling from the same generator. Trade-offs: single source reduces duplication and makes retry semantics central. It requires careful backpressure mapping for browser ReadableStream pull() semantics.

2) Backpressure mapping: Node async iteration implicitly handles backpressure by awaiting yield consumption. For ReadableStream pull(), we will buffer up to N token-chunks (N default 16) then pause reading from the socket. We chose a small memory buffer to avoid token accumulation and to let the runtime reclaim slot-based buffers.

3) Retry and de-duplication: on transient connection errors (5xx, ECONNRESET, network timeout), the internal source will attempt up to 2 automatic reconnect attempts with an exponential backoff (200ms -> 500ms). The server provides a 'resume_cursor' token index in the stream control events. We will resume from the last acknowledged token index. If no cursor is available, we fall back to server side resume (model replay start-token) and mark the retry as "best-effort" in telemetry. User-visible API exposes retry policy override and allows caller to opt-out. Risk: without precise server side cursors some tokens may be redelivered; we will dedupe on the client by token-id when present and provide an option to de-dupe by suffix-match for text streams.

4) Cancellation and cleanup: aborting an AsyncIterator (via return()) or ReadableStream.cancel() will signal the internal AbortController and synchronously close the underlying transport. We will emit a final event to the server for metrics and then cleanup. Important: return()/cancel() must not throw during cleanup — they should surface a promise that resolves when cleanup completes.

5) Ergonomics: provide examples: (A) simple for-await-of loop, (B) fetch-style pipeTo usage for browser uploads to DOM or downstream transforms, (C) attachable progress callback for UI streaming. Keep the surface API minimal: client.stream(params) returns an object { asAsyncIterable(), asReadableStream(), cancel(), onRetry(cb) }.

Acceptance criteria and observable targets (see list below).
acceptance_criteria: SDK exposes a single streaming entrypoint with two adapters: asAsyncIterable() and asReadableStream().
Backpressure mapping prevents unbounded memory growth in both Node and browser (memory regression < 10%).
Automatic retries occur for transient errors and resume logic uses server-provided resume_cursor when available.
Cancellation via iterator.return() and ReadableStream.cancel() triggers underlying transport close and resolves cleanup promise within 500ms under typical networks.
Comprehensive unit tests for adapter boundaries and an integration test against staging endpoint that simulates two disconnects with resumption.
Public docs and a migration example are checked into docs/sdk/streams and referenced in the changelog for ts-sdk-2.4.0.
